whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text:
Hi, I'm Emily Anderson. This is Greetings from the Canal. As you can see, it's outside. It's a piece designed for Annabelle Basin, which is the body of water outside of Plaxol Gallery.
I made it on site from the window that the projector is pointing out of in the space. We're standing right now outside of the Plaxol building.
And in making the piece, I did some research on the various fish that live in the Hudson River, the history of the basin.
This used to be an industrial area, and the basin was actually dug by an oil man, last name Annabelle, for the parking of oil barges in the canal.
So sort of a loading, unloading, unloading thing.
And it was a loading zone that was rife with pollution and continues to be very dirty.
So in the piece, you'll see little portholes appear to kind of reveal different fish of the basin.
I think one of my favorite ones, and he gets the most airtime, is a fish called the feather blenny.
And this fish is known for picking fight or bigger fish.
And I thought it was like a very New York kind of thing to include. So he's in there looking real tough.
Other ones that have good names are there's a fish called the hog choker,
which farmers would use to help fertilize their fish.
And then when the pigs would come out, they'd be like, oh, this dirt smells like fish.
I'm going to try to eat this and end up choking on the scales.
It's so disgusting and very weird.
And I feel like it's one of those things that a lot of people don't know is swimming around right near us.
Speaking about light in the piece, I really enjoyed the way light reflected off of the water of the basin when I was making it.
And so at the end of the six minute loop, there's about a minute and a half of just like a low light.
Kind of shining on the water.
So you can see the movement of the space.
And part of my hope in the piece is there's a door of the gallery that's next to the projector.
And it invites people to come outside, kind of stand by the canal basin and sort of look at it and think about the waterways of New York.
And I think that's a really good idea.
